title: Influence maximization in unknown social networks: Learning Policies for Effective Graph Sampling
venue: AAMAS 2020 (19th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems, Auckland); arXiv:1907.11625v5

research_question: Can deep reinforcement learning learn a network-discovery (node-querying) policy, under a budget of 5 queries from 5 random seeds, such that the 10 seeds chosen by greedy influence maximization on the discovered subgraph spread further in the full unknown network than the CHANGE sampling heuristic?
data: Four network families, each split into train and test networks (Table 1). Rural (microfinance diffusion in Indian villages, Banerjee et al. 2013): train rural1, rural2; test rural3, rural4. Animal (vole wildlife contact networks, Davis et al. 2015): train voles1, voles2; test voles3, voles4. Retweet (Twitter retweet networks, Network Data Repository, Rossi and Ahmed 2015): train copen, occupy; test israel (spelled isreal in Table 1), damascus. Homeless (HIV intervention campaigns for homeless youth in Los Angeles, Wilder et al. 2018): train a1, spy, mfp; test b1, cg1, node4, mfp2, mfp3, spy2, spy3. Totals: 9 training networks, 13 test networks. Unit is the network (graph); node counts, edge counts and collection periods are not reported in the text. Synthetic graphs: 5 SBM (or SSM for retweets) graphs per training graph, with Louvain communities. No individual-level sample size is given.
method: Markov decision process over the discovered subgraph: state is the discovered graph, action is querying an unqueried node, reward is the influence of the final seed set in the full graph at episode end (scaled by Eq. 1 using CHANGE and OPT) plus small per-step rewards for new nodes (Eq. 2). The Geometric-DQN network takes a global graph embedding (GCN layers pooled with DiffPool) plus per-node action embeddings (DeepWalk, found vital for stable training; GCN action features were unstable) and outputs a Q-value per candidate node. Trained with epsilon-greedy DQN, prioritized experience replay and a target network, on a random graph per episode from the training set, with synthetic graphs used on half the episodes. Deployed with frozen weights. Influence oracle: greedy influence maximization on the observed graph (approximating OPT greedily). Diffusion: independent cascade model, p = 0.1, budget 10 activated nodes, T = 5 queries. Baselines: CHANGE (query a random neighbour of each random seed; chosen over random greedy, snowball and recommend, which were 3.9, 42.1 and 41.7 percent worse). Two hand-designed heuristics H1 (query minimum-degree node) and H2 (minimum-degree node among those discovered in the last step) were used for insight analysis.
identification: Not a causal design. The comparison is algorithmic: policies trained on train networks are evaluated on held-out test networks of the same family, with the same budget, diffusion model and oracle as the baseline. Scores are averages over 100 diffusion simulations. No statistical tests, confidence intervals or seeds-variance reporting appear in the text.
scope: Social and interaction networks from four domains (rural households, wild voles, Twitter retweets, homeless youth contact networks). Transfer is tested within family only (train on one family's networks, test on that family's held-out networks). Dates of the datasets are not stated. Authors from IIT Madras, McGill University and Mila, and Harvard CRCS. No live field deployment is reported; the paper argues the setting resembles real deployment.
theory: Independent cascade diffusion (Kempe et al. 2003, 2005) and greedy influence maximization; friendship paradox (Feld 1991) motivates CHANGE; community structure motivates stochastic block models; MDP and POMDP framing for multi-graph training; deep Q-learning with graph representation learning.
measures: Influence score (mean nodes activated over 100 independent-cascade runs); improve percent (scaled reward: (influence minus CHANGE) divided by (OPT minus CHANGE)); per-step reward; true degree and true betweenness centrality of queried nodes; average improve percent per family.

key_findings.finding: Best Geometric-DQN variant beats CHANGE on all 13 reported test networks (e.g. voles4 80.2 vs 58.9; damascus 119.3 vs 95.24; israel 43.6 vs 30.6; voles3 45.8 vs 33.7; rural4 35.7 vs 31.5). Note the variant is the best one per test network as reported.
key_findings.numbers: Table 2 raw influence scores; OPT for voles4 115.7 and damascus 195.4

key_findings.finding: Average improve percent for the best variant per family is Rural 23.76, Animals 26.6, Retweet 19.7, Homeless 7.91. The Results text says 7-26 percent improvement, while the abstract, contributions list and conclusion say 7-23 percent: an internal inconsistency.
key_findings.location: Section 5 Results, Table 4; abstract; Section 1 contribution (4); Section 7 conclusion

key_findings.finding: Text claims training on multiple networks beats the average of single-network models on all but one family. Reading Table 3 as extracted, multiple-network training is lower on rural3 (10.26 vs 13.14 individual) and spy2 (20.76 vs 21.40), so the exceptions appear to be two. The column alignment comes from text extraction and should be checked against the PDF.
key_findings.numbers: Individual averages 13.14 and 21.40 vs multiple 10.26 and 20.76 on rural3 and spy2; e.g. b1 4.76 vs 14.29; mfp3 7.18 vs 18.10

key_findings.finding: Models trained only on synthetic SBM or SSM graphs score higher on average than the average of models trained on individual real networks. For Homeless networks, synthetic-only gives the highest average score. Adding synthetic graphs to real training data improved Homeless, Retweet and Rural results versus real-only training.
key_findings.numbers: No numeric values in the text; results are shown only in Figure 4

key_findings.finding: Heuristic H2 (minimum-degree node among those discovered in the last step) beats CHANGE on Animals, Retweet and some Homeless networks: voles4 72.8 vs 58.9; damascus 104.9 vs 95.2; israel 34.2 vs 30.6; b1 19.4 vs 19.1; spy2 16.4 vs 16.01. H1 is comparable to CHANGE. The text says H2 wins by huge margins on Homeless, but the Homeless gaps in Table 5 are small.
key_findings.numbers: Table 5 values quoted in finding; CHANGE, H1, H2, Geometric-DQN per graph

key_findings.finding: Geometric-DQN policies almost always discover larger graphs than CHANGE, but across Geometric-DQN policies there is no correlation between influence score and the size of the discovered graph.
key_findings.location: Section 6 Insights, Size of discovered graph

key_findings.finding: Two recurring behaviours in deployment: O1, the next node selected has minimum degree; O2, the node selected is among the most recently discovered. O2 almost always co-occurs with O1.
key_findings.location: Section 6 Insights, Observations on node selection; Figure 5 toy example

key_findings.finding: Geometric-DQN queries nodes with higher true degree and true betweenness centrality than CHANGE on b1 and israel, especially in the last query. H2 raises betweenness over CHANGE but not degree.
key_findings.numbers: Values appear only in figures; not extracted

key_findings.finding: Among four sampling baselines, Random greedy, Snowball and Recommend are 3.9, 42.1 and 41.7 percent worse than CHANGE, which is why CHANGE was the only baseline kept. The metric behind these percentages is not defined in the text.

Step rewards are about two orders of magnitude smaller than the final influence reward. The authors say they are essential for initial stable learning and suspect their role fades after early training.

Using DeepWalk embeddings as action inputs was vital for stable training; using GCN node features for actions gave unstable training because the action space is non-stationary across graphs. Neighbourhood DeepWalk was also cheaper than structural encodings.
Scaling the reward relative to CHANGE and OPT lets training pool graphs of different sizes and densities into one replay buffer; the paper treats this as the key enabler of multi-network training.
key_findings.location: Section 3.1, Rewards when using multiple graphs (Eq. 1)

limitations: OPT is approximated by greedy influence maximization because exact optimization is NP-hard, and the reward depends on CHANGE as the normalizing baseline (Eq. 1).
Table 2 and Table 4 report the best-performing Geometric-DQN variant per test network or test set. The text does not say how the variant was chosen, so these figures may be optimistic.
Environment parameters are fixed (ICM p = 0.1, budget 10, 5 seeds, T = 5 queries); sensitivity to these settings is not reported.
Multi-graph training turns the problem into a POMDP rather than an MDP, which the authors handle by reward scaling without a formal guarantee.
The authors say there is no correlation between performance and discovered graph size, and state that a detailed investigation of the learned patterns is left for future work.
Synthetic-graph results are reported only as a figure with no numbers in the text.
Homeless family is small (3 training and 7 test networks) and the paper gives no node counts or collection periods for any network.
Only the independent cascade model is evaluated; no other diffusion models and no live field deployment are tested.
Text inconsistency: 7-26 percent (Results) vs 7-23 percent (abstract, contributions, conclusion). The paper has no explicit limitations section.

Wilder et al. 2018 (AAMAS, End-to-end influence maximization in the field) - source of CHANGE, the baseline.
Kempe, Kleinberg and Tardos 2003 and 2005 - independent cascade model and greedy influence maximization.
Perozzi et al. 2014 (DeepWalk) - node embeddings used as action inputs.
Ying et al. 2018 (DiffPool) - hierarchical graph pooling for the global state.
Kipf and Welling 2016 (GCN) - graph convolution layers.
Mnih et al. 2015 (DQN) and Schaul et al. 2016 (prioritized replay) - training machinery.
Khalil et al. 2017 - RL for combinatorial graph problems (closest prior work, but on fully observed graphs).
Feld 1991 (friendship paradox) and Holland et al. 1983 (stochastic block models) - conceptual basis of CHANGE and synthetic graphs.
Banerjee et al. 2013 (diffusion of microfinance) and Wilder et al. 2018 (HIV campaigns) - source datasets.
